newsitem.title: GUATEMALA: Amnesty agreement disappoints some Guatemalans.
newsitem.headline: Amnesty agreement disappoints some Guatemalans.

text.p: Human rights and church leaders said on Thursday they were disappointed with the terms of a limited amnesty contained in a peace accord signed by the government and guerrilla commanders in Madrid.

"Instead of bringing reconciliation to Guatemalans this will bring confrontation. And it is totally frustrating to me that the government is saying this is not a general amnesty," Karen Fischer, spokeswoman for the Alliance Against Impunity.
President Alvaro Arzu and government and guerrilla peace negotiators said the agreement was not a general amnesty and would not continue the tradition of impunity for Guatemala's armed forces.

The accord signed in Madrid earlier on Thursday is a final precursor to a definitive peace treaty scheduled to be signed in Guatemala City on Dec. 29, which will end Central America's longest and last civil war.
The amnesty detailed in the accord exempts from criminal prosecution guerrillas who committed so-called political crimes including rebellion, sedition and illegal arms possession.

Guerrilla and army personnel, who fought a war in which tens of thousands of civilians were assassinated, "disappeared," tortured and massacred, are also exempted from prosecution for common crimes directly connected to the rebellion or the counterinsurgency.
"They left it so vague that you can include any type of common crimes that according to them are linked to the armed conflict. You can say anything is connected," said Fischer.

"Under this legal shield some serious crimes could remain unpunished. We believe that it puts political interests above historical, moral and legal ones," said Carlos Adana, spokesman for the Archbishopric.
According to the agreement the amnesty will not cover crimes against humanity -- such as genocide and other crimes defined in international treaties that Guatemala has ratified.
The accord also recognises the right of victims to compensation for damages from the war.
The amnesty is outlined in three pages of the 15-page document signed in Madrid that also contains the terms for the legal reincorporation of guerrilla fighters into civilian life in Guatemala.
In the agreement the government promises to promote in Congress a bill for a National Reconciliation Law which will make the amnesty into law.
